slides.text: In 1970, Philips installed a robot that leaned toward quiet voices and drew back from shouting.
Edward Ihnatowicz built it for the Evoluon, Philips’ exhibition hall in Eindhoven: a hydraulic steel skeleton taller than anyone who came to see it.
Four microphones and two Doppler radar units in its head picked up sound and movement in the room.
A Philips computer read them, and the neck turned the head toward gentle sounds and pulled it back from loud ones.
Philips took it down in 1974. Its steel skeleton then stood outdoors in Zeeland for more than 40 years.
In 2017, a university in Kraków acquired the skeleton and took it to Poland to bring it back to life.
For the friend who lowers their voice around animals.
slides.sub: Field Notes — kinetic history, from ART Lab
